Lofos Kapi: Before and After the Holocaust of Kalavryta

The hill of Kapi in Kalavryta changed from an everyday landscape into a place of execution and, later, a memorial site. Maps, photographs and local commemorations trace that transformation after December 1943.

Kalavryta under occupation

PANAGIOTA KATSARAMENIDOU

«Lofos Kapi- Before and after the Holocaust of Kalavryta»

In Greece during World War II, the German occupation lasted from April 1941

to October 1944. During this period, Nazi forces committed atrocities and mass

executions of civilian populations, looting and destroying villages and settlements. One

region in Greece, in the Prefecture of Achaea, that suffered a devastating blow during

the German occupation is the small town of Kalavryta as well as its broader

surrounding area.

Map 1. Map of Greece highlighting the location of Kalavryta1

02

The massacre and its location

The Holocaust of Kalavryta was part of the Wehrmacht military operation

targeted against ELAS forces operating in the area. "Operation Kalavryta" was planned

on November 25, 1943, by the commander of the 117th Jäger Division, Karl von Le

Suire, and was carried out by the Kampfgruppen (battle groups) led by Woelffinger,

Ebersberger, and Gnass. The German forces claimed that the destruction of Kalavryta

constituted retaliation for the execution of 86 German prisoners of war by the partisans.

The execution of the Germans took place on December 7, 1943, after the order for

"Operation Kalavryta" had already been drafted under the directives of Le Suire

(Lazaris, 2018: 66-67).

The bloodiest act of "Operation Kalavryta" was the execution of the male

population of Kalavryta and neighboring areas, which took place on Kapi2 Hill (Lofos

Kapi). The hill is located approximately 700 meters from Kalavryta, overlooking the

town center.

Map 2. Kalavryta and the Site of Sacrifice. 3

In the present paper, reference will be made to the landscape and to local history,

exploring how the hill transformed its status following the execution: evolving from a

simple field into a site of execution, a place for holding memorial services

2 This locaƟon was formerly known to locals as Kapis' Field, Kapis' Hill, or Kapis' Hollow (Kapis or Kappis being the owner of the plot). 3 Archaeological Cadastre

03

From field to memorial

for the victims of the Occupation, and

nowadays a historical site requiring special state protection, as a location "directly

linked to the memory of the local inhabitants as well as the entirety of Greece" as the

site of one of the bloodiest mass crimes of Nazism against a civilian population

(Government Gazette of the Hellenic Republic, 1993). This research was based on the

photographic archive of the Municipal Museum of the Kalavrytians Holocaust.

Following the Occupation, this specific location was delineated and gradually began

acquiring its contemporary layout.

Chronicle of the site’s development

In 1959, the Cross was constructed at the top of the Execution Site by the

Municipality of Kalavryta. The following year (1960), sculptor Anna Vafia created the

"Sculpture of the Grief-Stricken Mother" (Figure 7)—a symbolic statue of the

Kalavrytian mother, conveying a intense sense of loss that radiates outward through the

depiction of the mother embracing her dead child. In the early 1970s, based on designs

by Ilias Skroumbelos, Christos Iakovidis, and Giannis Liapis, the monument that

continues to adorn the hill to this day was constructed (Figure 8).

It consists of the Cross at the hilltop, while in the lower section, it features slabs

of varying dimensions bearing the names and ages of the executed and the survivors,

as well as a cenotaph containing the oil lamps (vigil lights) of the families. The

arrangement of the slabs is designed to symbolize the siege/encirclement in which the

people of Kalavryta found themselves under German forces prior to their execution, as

well as the broader encirclement experienced by Greece during the Occupation. At the

Execution Site, there are also graves of the executed, created by their relatives in the

immediate days following the execution.

Throughout December, as well as annually, commemorative events take place

in Kalavryta and the surrounding villages. On December 13, the primary event includes

a memorial service held at the Metropolitan Church of Kalavryta. An address follows

inside the church (typically delivered by a survivor or a descendant of the executed),

and after the conclusion of the ceremony and speech, a procession departs from the

church toward the Municipal Museum of the Kalavrytan Holocaust. Passing through its

courtyard, the procession continues to the Execution Site, retracing the exact path taken

by the residents of Kalavryta on December 13, 1943.

04

Commemoration

At the Execution Site, wreaths are laid, and the Mayor of the town reads aloud

the names of the executed. This event serves as a preservation of memory for the

tragedy suffered by the town and the Greek nation as a whole, while on a broader scale,

it keeps alive in public memory the atrocities of an era that is distant, yet remains so

close.

Moreover, this event remains a constant reminder of memory's profound

capacity to color and sustain history, continuously reproducing it and cultivating deep-

rooted connections between people and their historical heritage.

Places, memory and interpretation

Kalavryta, Achaea, Greece from 13th of December 1943. The story situated in Kalavryta a greek small city in the prefecture of Achaia. The main historical fact is the massacre in 13th of December 1943. It concern more the local community how this fact and especially the memorial monument reminds at the local community the past and why people around the world visit the memorial monument. The story will be digital.

Public-history question

How has a site of Nazi violence become a place of public commemoration?
